anomaly_def.Name: Query Plan Selection Anomaly + Storage I/O Throughput Anomaly + Network and Connectivity Resource Anomaly
anomaly_def.Description:
Query Plan Selection Anomaly: The optimizer persistently selects sub-optimal execution plans even though statistics are adequate, leading to disproportionate resource consumption per statement.
Storage I/O Throughput Anomaly: The physical storage layer cannot deliver the read/write throughput, IOPS, or latency required by the workload, producing device-level wait inflation.
Network and Connectivity Resource Anomaly: Client–server transport or connection-handling capacity is exhausted, causing connection establishment delays, socket backlog growth, and stalled data transfer.

When all three root causes coexist, the database exhibits compound symptoms: queries flip to full-table scans or poorly chosen join orders that inflate page reads; the surge in random and sequential I/O collides with an already saturated storage subsystem, driving disk queues and read/write latencies even higher. Prolonged statement runtimes hold server processes and sockets open, so listener backlogs, half-open TCP sessions, and client-side timeouts escalate. End-to-end response times swing wildly, and performance graphs show intertwined peaks of I/O waits, client-read/client-write waits, and hard-parse or plan-change events. Administrators may mis-attribute slowdowns to a single layer because each bottleneck masks and amplifies the others.

Causally, a bad plan is the spark: it multiplies physical I/O demand, pushing the storage layer past its throughput ceiling. The resulting I/O stalls extend query execution and result-set streaming time, which ties up server worker threads and keeps network sockets active longer. As active connections swell and data trickles slowly over the congested network, handshake retries and backlog overflows appear, feeding further delays that lengthen query runtimes and increase optimizer re-parses, perpetuating the selection of the same poor plan. This feedback loop between plan inefficiency, storage saturation, and network congestion degrades overall capacity far more severely than any single anomaly acting alone.

entry.official_description: Semisync replica socket fd is %u. select() cannot handle if the socket fd is bigger than %u (FD_SETSIZE).
entry.cause_analysis: The failure is typically associated with connection establishment, authentication exchange, protocol correctness, network reachability, or client/server communication stability.
entry.solution_guidance: Check endpoint reachability, authentication flow, connection limits, protocol compatibility, transport stability, and client connection lifecycle management.
